claims.feature: glimpsed threads of a larger tapestry
claims.claim: Hromic (via Wikipedia) describes the usual sense of far more in the background than told, glimpsing a few shining threads in a larger tapestry.
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Last Light of the Sun (Reception citing Hromic, Dusmann)
claims.quote: glimpsing a few shining threads in a larger tapestry

claims.feature: weak magic keyed to romance sources
claims.claim: Ringel notes magic in Arbonne is weak, no wizard's duels, in keeping with the scarcity of pagan marvels in real medieval romances.
claims.source: Faye Ringel, 'Kay's Provence: From Arbonne to Ysabel' (ICFA 2009 / Anticipation 2009 paper)

claims.claim: Ringel reads Arbonne and Ysabel as portraying Provence as a palimpsest where older history bleeds through into the present.
claims.source: Faye Ringel, 'Kay's Provence: From Arbonne to Ysabel' (ICFA 2009 / Anticipation 2009 paper)
claims.quote: a palimpsest of time and space

claims.claim: Ringel quotes Bethune that events separated by centuries are often collapsed into a single era while only the cultural milieu is kept.
claims.source: Faye Ringel, 'Kay's Provence: From Arbonne to Ysabel' (ICFA 2009 / Anticipation 2009 paper)
claims.quote: often collapsed into a single era

claims.claim: Ringel shows Kay transforming troubadour poems (Peire Vidal, Bernart de Ventadorn) into the in-world song of the title.
claims.source: Faye Ringel, 'Kay's Provence: From Arbonne to Ysabel' (ICFA 2009 / Anticipation 2009 paper)
claims.quote: transforms these and other troubadour poems

claims.claim: Tarantino's essay characterises Kay's writing as elegiac and gently melancholy, turning on memory, continuity and the consequences of conduct (read via summary; quote withheld).
claims.source: Bob Tarantino, 'The fantastic fiction of Guy Gavriel Kay', C2C Journal (2016-09-07)

claims.claim: Randall states that in the passage narrating Darien's death in The Darkest Road the sentences are short and the description concrete.
claims.quote: Sentences are short, description is concrete.

claims.claim: Randall describes the tone of that same Darien death passage as matter-of-fact.
Randall reads the passage narrating the departure of Arthur, Lancelot and Guinevere as a deliberate reach for rhetorical high style, in contrast with the plain Darien passage.
claims.quote: the language here is an obvious attempt at rhetorical

claims.claim: Randall explains the elevated register of the Arthurian departure scene as a consequence of who perceives it, not of the event's importance.
claims.quote: because it is perceived by minds capable of comprehending magnificence

claims.claim: Randall counts twenty-six different agents of focalization in The Fionavar Tapestry.
claims.quote: employs twenty-six different agents of focalization
claims.page: opening section, before 'Assimilating the Secondary World'

claims.claim: Randall counts twenty-one shifts of focalization in the eighth chapter of The Summer Tree.
Randall counts eighty-seven shifts of focalization across Darien's search for Rakoth, with Darien himself the focalizant only nine of those times.
claims.quote: the narrative shifts focalization eighty-seven times

claims.claim: Randall argues that Kay's shifts of focalization delay the unfolding of the story as well as advancing it.
claims.quote: the shifts delay the unfolding of the story

claims.claim: Randall argues the reader must assemble Kay's secondary world by inference from the successive focalizations rather than from direct exposition.
claims.quote: Our task is to piece together the world by understanding the focalizations.

verdicts.trueWording: "the sense of glimpsing a few shining threads in a larger tapestry"
verdicts.note: Raw en.wikipedia.org page, Reception section, fetched live (HTTP 200). Quotes SF Site reviewer Alma H. Hromic: "There is the usual sense that there is more, so much more, in the background of this story than the reader has been told -- the sense of glimpsing a few shining threads in a larger tapestry. A book to savour." Both limbs (usual sense of far more in the background; shining threads in a larger tapestry) present verbatim; Dusmann/Quill & Quire is the adjacent citation, as the source line says.

verdicts.trueWording: "magic is 'weak' in Arbonne ... there are no wizard's duels"
verdicts.note: Raw brightweavings.com/kaysprovence/ fetched live (HTTP 200); byline 'Faye Ringel, Ph.D.', paper presented at ICFA March 2009 and Anticipation August 2009, matching the source line. Page: "magic is 'weak' in Arbonne-belief may be strong, but there are no wizard's duels, in keeping with the relatively small amount of 'merveilleux paien' [pagan miracles or marvels ...] in the real Medieval romances." Every limb (weak magic, no wizard's duels, scarcity of pagan marvels in real medieval romances) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: "portray Provence as a palimpsest of time and space"
verdicts.note: Same raw Ringel page. Full sentence: "Both A Song for Arbonne and Ysabel portray Provence as a palimpsest of time and space, where the older history frequently bleeds through into the present time, and the simultaneity can be dizzying." Both novels named, and the bleed-through-into-the-present limb is explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: "events separated by centuries ... often collapsed into a single era"
verdicts.note: Same raw Ringel page. Ringel quotes Brian Bethune (Maclean's, 'The Man Who Sailed'): "that general cultural milieu is all he adopts from his sources. Everything else is altered to fit the needs of the story: rulers, religions, geography, even the chronology - events separated by centuries in actual history are often collapsed into a single era." Attribution to Bethune-via-Ringel and the 'only the cultural milieu is kept' limb are both explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: "Kay brilliantly transforms these and other troubadour poems"
verdicts.note: Same raw Ringel page: "Kay brilliantly transforms these and other troubadour poems into the veritable 'Song for Arbonne' of the title." The antecedent 'these' is the two poems quoted immediately above: Peire Vidal's ('I breathe in and draw toward me the air / That I feel coming from Provence') and the troubadour Kay names in his own journal entry. One spelling divergence, not a limb failure: the page spells him 'Bernart de Ventadour', the claim 'Bernart de Ventadorn' (standard variant of the same troubadour; the page also cites his Canso 60, 'Quan la frej'aura venta').

verdicts.trueWording: "elegiac tone and the gentle melancholy of farewells"
verdicts.note: Raw c2cjournal.ca article fetched live (HTTP 200); byline 'Bob Tarantino, September 7, 2016', matching the source line. No quote was tendered with the claim, so it cannot be graded VERBATIM, but the raw page (not a summary) supports every limb, in wording close to the claim's own: "Kay's writings are suffused with an elegiac tone and the gentle melancholy of farewells"; "They turn on the foundational nature of memory and the continuity of human experience from age to age and land to land"; "Kay's most compelling stories demonstrate the consequences of conduct - the present of his stories is always a product of their past." The claim's parenthetical '(read via summary)' is now superseded: the raw page was reached.

Raw brightweavings.com/randallfionavar/ fetched live (HTTP 200); Randall, 'Shifting Focalization and the Strategy of Delay'. The sentence follows the block quotation of Darien's death in Starkadh cited as (DR, 366-7), introduced as 'Compare, for example, the style of Darien's passing with that of the departure of Arthur, Lancelot, and Guinevere. First Darien:'. Both limbs (short sentences, concrete description) and the passage's identity as the Darien death scene in The Darkest Road are on the page.

Same raw Randall page, two sentences after the index-171 quote and attached to the same DR 366-7 Darien death passage: "Sentences are short, description is concrete. Except for the first two and the last sentences, the scene is restricted to Darien's sensory perception. The tone, moreover, is matter-of-fact."

verdicts.trueWording: "the language here is an obvious attempt at rhetorical 'high style'"
verdicts.note: Same raw Randall page, following the block quotation of the Arthurian departure cited as (DR, 394): "Like the language of many other passages in the Tapestry (cf. Kevin's death, Paul's death on the Summer Tree, Diarmuid's death), the language here is an obvious attempt at rhetorical 'high style.'" The contrast limb is also explicit: 'By comparison, the departure of the Arthurian trio is much more magnificent' set against the Darien passage.

verdicts.trueWording: "more magnificent because it is perceived by minds capable of comprehending magnificence"
verdicts.note: Same raw Randall page: "The departure of the trio is more magnificent because it is perceived by minds capable of comprehending magnificence." The 'not of the event's importance' limb is supported in the immediately preceding sentences: 'for Fionavar the incident is less mythically significant than Darien's death. The difference lies in the focalization' - the departure shifts to an unspecified omniscient focalizant (Genette's zero focalization), whereas Darien's death is focalized through him.

verdicts.trueWording: "The Fionavar Tapestry employs twenty-six different agents of focalization (focalizants)"
verdicts.note: Same raw Randall page, in the opening section just before the four-fold effect list, as the page hint says. The sentence continues '...and even adds, in a very few places, an unspecified omniscient focalizant' - a rider that does not disturb the count of twenty-six named agents.

verdicts.trueWording: "the eighth of The Summer Tree, shifts focalization twenty-one times"
verdicts.note: Same raw Randall page: "Only three chapters in the entire trilogy are focalized through just one character, and one chapter, the eighth of The Summer Tree, shifts focalization twenty-one times." The next sentence adds the page span: 'shifting the focalization twenty-one times in twenty-four pages'.

verdicts.trueWording: "shifts focalization eighty-seven times, with Darien as focalizant only nine"
verdicts.note: Same raw Randall page, in 'The Strategy of Delay': "During Darien's search for Rakoth, the narrative shifts focalization eighty-seven times, with Darien as focalizant only nine of those times, usually in brief passages." Both figures (87 shifts, 9 Darien focalizations) are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: "the shifts delay the unfolding of the story"
verdicts.note: Same raw Randall page, fourth item of the four-fold effect list: "Fourth, and seemingly opposed to the third effect, the shifts delay the unfolding of the story; kernels that might occupy only a few pages if focalized through one character take several under the focalization of more than one." The 'as well as advancing it' limb is the third effect ('the constant shifting moves the novel from incident to incident, and in fact makes possible the co-ordination of important events') and is restated later as 'the strategy of shifting both advances and impedes the story's events'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'rather than from direct exposition' - the page never contrasts focalization with exposition or direct description of the world
verdicts.trueWording: "Our task is to piece together the world by understanding the focalizations."
verdicts.note: Quotation is verbatim on the raw Randall page and the assembling-by-inference limb is supported ('Kay's forces us to experience Fionavar as its many characters do'; the strategy 'controls the speed and the manner in which we assimilate the culture of Fionavar'). But the article contains no occurrence of 'exposition' at all, and the only contrast it draws is with fantasies focalized through one or two central characters, not with expository delivery. The nearest support is a different sentence, about events rather than the world: 'the shifting is necessary if we are to observe the kernels directly, instead of having them related by direct speech or another kind of sub-narration.' Graded PARTIAL rather than verified because the contrastive limb is an inference the page does not state.
